title: Show HN: Black Ops II statically recompiled to native ARM64 macOS
author: adrbn
body: I grew up with Black Ops 2 and wanted to see if I could make it work on my 2020 MacBook Pro. So I used Claude Opus 5.5 to create a tool that converts your copy of the game (from Steam) to a native ARM64 Mac app, with almost 60fps in all areas. The whole game is statically recompilated ahead-of-time (AOT) and does not use any emulator whatsoever, be it Wine, Crossover or Rosetta. The best thing is the performance, although some heat issues are still to fix. You get to play the whole Campaign, local Multiplayer (with bots) and local Zombies (all DLCs maps; you need to have them in your Steam library obviously) at about 60fps. Split-screen was not in the PC version, but I've been working on it lately; it's coming soon! LAN mode is on the roadmap for later too :)

title: Show HN: Crayon, the web's first personalized newspaper (1995), relaunched
author: mayyah42
body: In 1995 I co-built CRAYON (CReAte Your Own Newspaper) - the first personalized news service on the web. 650k people made papers. The Perl CGI site ran, barely, for 31 years. I've now rebuilt it: stories ranked by independent-source count instead of an editor or engagement algorithm, every side of every story on one page. Your 1996 password still works, and every subscriber can open their original paper as a time capsule - dead sources marked "lost to time."

comments.author: drrajvanshi
comments.text: Ranking by count of independent sources is a nice answer to engagement ranking. How do you decide two outlets are actually independent, though? A lot of "different" stories are the same wire copy lightly rewritten, so I'm curious how you dedupe that.

title: Show HN: Caramel: a speech-to-speech conversation model trained only on audio
author: naklecha
body: I trained a speech-to-speech model last night, inspired by Dessa. I'm calling the model caramel-1. The model learned from recordings of people talking and nothing else, and has never seen a single word of text. The code, the training recipe and the weights are open source.caramel-1 sounds incredibly human. Most of what caramel-1 says doesn't make sense yet, but the sentences make a little more sense every time I add more data.Caramel is fast. On a GPU, caramel-1 makes 1 second of audio in about 0.09 seconds, which is fast enough to talk to a real person live. It even works on my MacBook Pro (M3 Pro): running two copies at once, it makes 1 second of conversation in about 0.25 seconds.

## How these prices are measured

- Per GPU-hour. Clouds rent whole machines, so a machine's hourly price is divided by the GPUs in it (for example AWS p5.48xlarge, 8 × H100, ÷ 8). Compute only: storage, network and support are extra and differ by provider.
- List prices. AWS (US East, N. Virginia) and Azure (East US) on-demand Linux prices; RunPod Secure Cloud (its own data centres) and Community Cloud (third-party hosts). Committed-use and reserved prices are usually lower and are not shown.
- Marketplace. Vast.ai lists machines offered by many independent hosts worldwide; the median and the lowest per-GPU price of the rentable on-demand offers that day, with the number of offers. Few offers means the figure can swing.
- Checks. A list price that moves more than 50% in a day is held at the previous value until checked.

title: Show HN: HC – a HyperCard clone that runs original stacks on today's Macs
author: cleobuline
body:
HC: HyperCard brought back · Stacks, cards, buttons · What you click answers · Part of the Labynet citadel
◈ Labynet 
 Code-Rebirth 
 Code 
 Forums 
 Wiki 
FR 
 ☀️ 
Home 
HC
HyperCard for today's Mac
HyperCard pour le Mac d'aujourd'hui
Stacks, cards, buttons. The scripts of 1987 wake up on the Mac of
 2026, intact, as if they had only been asleep.
▼ Download HC 
 Demo stacks 
 ♥ Support HC 
Free software, free of charge · macOS 10.13 and later · Intel and Apple Silicon ·
 signed and notarised ·
 what's new 
The games, on video
Written in plain HyperTalk, and played in HC. Click a picture to watch
 the video; the stacks themselves are further down, in the
 demo stacks .
▶ 
The pinball 
 The ball knows nothing of the table: it feels its
 way ahead, and every mushroom carries its own script. 
 Written in plain HyperTalk. The ball
 knows nothing of the table: it feels its way ahead at every step,
 and every mushroom, every bumper, every target carries its own
 script. To add one, you copy it. 
▶ 
Tetris 
 The falling piece is a single polygon button; the
 board, a text of twenty lines. 
 Written in plain HyperTalk too. The
 falling piece is a single polygon button that changes shape at
 every rotation; the board is a plain text of twenty lines, and a
 full row is just a line of text that gets deleted. 
▶ 
Space Invaders 
 Forty polygon buttons, after Tomohiro Nishikado's
 monsters; the formation speeds up as it thins out. 
 Written in plain HyperTalk, as ever. The
 forty invaders are polygon buttons, drawn after Tomohiro
 Nishikado's little monsters; the formation moves as one, a plain
 set the loc per invader, and hurries as it thins
 out. 
▶ 
The brick breaker 
 Sixty rainbow bricks; off the edge of the paddle the
 ball flies at an angle, and every brick makes it faster. 
 Written in plain HyperTalk, like the
 others. The paddle and the ball are polygon buttons; the ball keeps
 its position in decimal numbers, rounded only for display. Off the
 middle of the paddle it goes straight back, off the edge up to
 sixty degrees, and every brick broken makes it a little
 faster. 
What HC does
It opens original HyperCard stacks , Apple's format from 1987
 to 1998, and runs their scripts as they are , with no
 conversion. On a corpus of real stacks, 99.7% of the scripts are
 accepted.
It is measured against the original. Every doubt is settled
 in the real HyperCard, under emulation, not from memory.
All of HyperCard, plus colour : paint, icons,
 backColor , foreColor , textColor .
 For games, polygon buttons and the keysDown .
Native and universal : a real Mac application, from High
 Sierra to today's Macs, signed by the Association Labynet and
 notarised by Apple. Free software, under the MIT licence.
Demo stacks
Download a stack, unzip it, then open it with HC: a double-click, or
 File › Open Stack… .
◉ Pinball
The pinball table from the video. The flippers are held with the
 W and N keys. It is a construction set:
 with the Button tool, copy a mushroom, paste it elsewhere, shape it
 with the mouse, and play.
▼ flipper.stack.zip 
✎ Hangman
The hangman game: a gallows, a word to find, twenty-six letters.
 Play with the mouse or the keyboard; seven mistakes and the little
 man is hanged. The whole game lives in the stack script: open it,
 and add your own words.
▼ pendu.stack.zip 
▦ Tetris
The Tetris we all know, in HyperTalk. The falling piece is a single
 polygon button that changes shape at every rotation. Play with the
 arrow keys, or with Q D to move,
 Z to rotate, X to drop faster, and space
 to let go. The whole game lives in the stack script.
▼ Tetris.stack.zip 
▲ Space Invaders
Forty invaders made of polygon buttons, moving as one and speeding
 up as you shoot them down. Four shelters that crumble, a saucer
 that flies by now and then. Play with the arrow keys, or with
 Q D to move and Z or space
 to fire. The whole game lives in the stack script. The house
 record: 1,470 points.
▼ SpaceInvaders.stack.zip 
▬ Brick breaker
Sixty bricks in the colours of the rainbow, a paddle and a ball
 made of polygon buttons. Off the middle of the paddle the ball goes
 straight back, off the edge it flies at an angle, up to sixty
 degrees; it speeds up a little with every brick. Play with the
 arrow keys, or with Q D to move, and
 Z or space to launch the ball.
▼ CasseBriques.stack.zip 
◆ Boulder-Prout
A red-haired digger, boulders and diamonds: a homemade Boulder
 Dash, loosely inspired. Every cell is a button carrying a colour
 icon. Boulders fall and roll, but only a falling one crushes.
 Fireflies explode on contact, and a crushed butterfly turns into
 diamonds. Three caves, each one drawn as text in a hidden field.
 Play with the arrow keys, or with W A 
 S D ; R restarts the cave.
 It needs HC 0.8.8.
▼ BoulderProut.stack.zip 
● Gobe-Prout
A chomper, dots, four ghosts: a homemade Pac-Man, loosely
 inspired. The maze is our own, and each ghost hunts its own way:
 red charges, pink cuts you off, cyan closes in from the other
 side, orange dawdles. A power pellet turns them blue and edible.
 The characters are colour-icon buttons, moved point by point. Play
 with the arrow keys, or with W A 
 S D . It needs HC 0.8.8.
▼ GobeProut.stack.zip 
✦ Astro-Prout
A ship, rocks, a saucer: a homemade Asteroids, loosely inspired,
 drawn entirely in white-outlined polygon buttons. The ship turns
 and drifts on its momentum, space wraps around at the edges, rocks
 break in two and then in four, and the heartbeat speeds up.
 ← → or A D to
 turn, ↑ or W to thrust, space to fire,
 ↓ or S for hyperspace. It needs HC 0.8.8.
▼ AstroProut.stack.zip 
▣ Pousse-Prout
A red-haired pusher, crates and targets: a homemade Sokoban.
 Thirteen warehouses, every one solved by the computer before it
 went into the stack. A crate can be pushed, never pulled, so it
 gets stuck fast. Play with the arrow keys, or W 
 A S D ; U undoes
 a move, R restarts, and a click on a square walks the
 pusher there by the shortest path. The levels are written in XSB
 notation in hidden fields, so a level found elsewhere pastes right
 in. It needs HC 0.8.8.
▼ PousseProut.stack.zip 
▤ Lingot-Prout
A runner, gold bars and guards: a homemade Lode Runner, on the
 original's 28 by 16 board. Run, climb, hang from the bars, and dig
 the brick to the left ( X ) or to the right
 ( C ): guards fall into the hole… which fills back in
 after nine seconds. Take the last gold bar and a hidden ladder
 appears. Eight levels. Run with the arrow keys, or W 
 A S D ; R 
 restarts the level. It needs HC 0.8.8.
▼ LingotProut.stack.zip 
Share your stack
Made a stack with HC, a game, a tool, a curiosity? Send it in: the
 best ones will join the demo stacks, with your name.
Compress your stack into a .zip (right-click ›
 Compress in the Finder).
Attach it to an email, with your name or nickname and a line to
 say what it does.
✉ Send my stack 
patricia [at] labynet [dot] fr
Every stack is opened and read before it is published. 
 A stack contains scripts: we check that it does nothing harmful
 before offering it to others.
Support HC
HC is free and will stay free. If you like it, you can help it grow:
 every donation, even a small one, funds its development.
♥ Make a donation 
Donations go through PayPal
Installing
Download the
 DMG of the latest release 
 (earlier ones are on the releases page ).
Open it, and drag HC.app into Applications .
Launch HC. The first time, macOS asks: "HC is an app downloaded
 from the Internet. Are you sure you want to open it?". Click
 Open : it asks only once.
Signed by the Association Labynet, notarised by Apple. 
 Since release 0.8.3, macOS has checked HC: no more "damaged" message,
 no more command to type.
 For a release older than 0.8.3 ,
 which is not notarised, macOS still says "HC is damaged" — it is
 not. Once, in the Terminal:
xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/HC.app

title: Show HN: Vaultbase – a self-hosted back end in a single binary
author: khalidsheet
body:
One binary to run and you have a full backend at your fingertips: a database with a REST API, sign-in, realtime, files, server-side hooks and jobs, on SQLite or Postgres. It's MIT licensed.
You can try the demo at https://demo.vaultbase.sh (the login is filled in, and it resets every hour).
I built it to ship fast. I always tend to write the same logic for any new project, whether it's a side project or a small to medium project for a client. I wanted something my friends and I could work with fast, try new things with, and that's easy to use. Then it became something I really wanted to work on and make as complete as I can for any type of backend.
As of writing this post it has 80 releases since May this year and is backed by more than 2,800 tests. I also run security reviews with Claude and fix what they find. It hasn't had an outside audit yet.
It was built with the help of Claude, from the codebase to the documentation and fact-checking it against the code. Claude helped speed up the pace, find bugs, and write tests.
Vaultbase is pre-1.0, so expect some bugs and issues here and there. I'm working hard to fix each and every one of them.
Thank you for taking the time to read this. I'd really appreciate any feedback, even if you didn't like Vaultbase. The demo is yours to try, and it's two commands to run locally.

title: Show HN: Rystic – Stateful Local Simulators of Slack, GitHub and Linear
author: evan_whitehouse
body: Hi HN, we're Zach and Evan, founders of Rystic (https://www.rystic.ai). As LLMs have progressed, producing code has become fast and cheap but verification has not. At my previous company I noticed that whenever I could test a service locally or in CI this bottleneck went away. If a service needed to use a shared sandbox or staging environment to run integration tests, verification was a huge pain. At Rystic we are taking that idea and applying it to every third-party service. We are trying to give developers a way to verify that their code works without calling real systems.To do this, we build deterministic simulators of APIs like Slack, Stripe and S3. You can control these locally; set their state and inspect it. Our aim is to make these a controllable stand-in for the real service, much more so than any sandbox. For this we offer fault injection, latency injection and multiple actor support. So for example you can cancel a subscription mid-cycle as the customer in the billing portal, then check that your app handles the proration and removes access. In the Stripe sandbox someone has to click through the portal by hand.We recreate these applications as Go binaries to make them performant. A single simulator can handle thousands of requests per second. You can even control whether they get rate limited or not depending on how realistic you want your test to be.To make the simulators we construct a set of tests based on their docs, probe their API, gather traces then use that to reverse engineer the state transitions of the application. Then we iterate on this by running deterministic tests and actively trying to break it. Proving this state machine is the same as the original would be NP hard but we can still show that they are equivalent over several hundred multi-step workflows. To make sure that our version stays accurate we test every night to catch drift and repair it. Each simulator's fidelity card lists its score, which is how closely it matches the real API across those workflows, and we share the failing tests with customers: https://www.rystic.ai/simulatorsIt is frustrating to have these incredibly powerful tools for producing code but then be left with the annoying work of verifying that what is produced actually works. No one wants to spend their day finding API keys, setting up sandbox accounts and manually clicking through applications. We are trying to make a future where that does not happen, where you can move fast and not break things.We would love for you to give it a try. Any feedback is very welcome.Here's a quick video on using the Slack twin to run evals: https://youtu.be/qwin0LAeaeUInstall:curl -fsSL https://www.rystic.ai/install.sh | shbrew install rystic-inc/tap/rysticor download a binary with checksums from https://github.com/Rystic-Inc/rystic/releases.Free: the Slack, GitHub and Linear simulators. No card needed. Everything else is $90 a month, and code HACKERNEWS will get you a month free.Current simulators: Stripe, Slack, GitHub, Kalshi, PayPal, Lob, Okta, Linear, Resend, Anthropic, Clerk, Dropbox, Gmail, Google Drive, Notion, S3, Shopify Storefront, Word.Coming: OpenAI, ElevenLabs, NetSuite, QuickBooks, Square, Sentry, PostHog.We are rapidly adding more to our catalog and if there are any that you would like to see added, please let us know in the comments.

title: Show HN: Mimzie, an agent-neutral alternative to the Claude Suite/Claude Cowork
author: kyleandruczk
body:
hi HN!I built Mimzie, an agent neutral AI workspace inspired by the Claude Suite (Docs, Sheets, Slides) and Cowork.It's a free desktop app that runs ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok in their native CLI harnesses. Think T3 Code or Conductor but for knowledge work. It's basically a GUI for managing knowledge work agents in various form factors. One of those form factors is Bots, akin to Grok Bot or Dots.The original idea for mimzie was simple: I pay for Claude and ChatGPT, and a lot of my day-to-day work lives in .xlsx, .pptx and .docx files. Moreover, I was sick and tired of losing context between AI platforms. I didn't want to bet the house on one AI lab's product, be it the ChatGPT or the Claude Desktop app.So I built an AI desktop app that was agent neutral.The goal of mimzie is to bring the kind of agent workflows that devs have had with codex and claude code into the hands of everyone. And to have a friendly GUI to do it. I've found that the personal agents, hermes and openclaw, are intimidating to set up and confusing to the average non-technical person.some of the core principles of mimzie:- your file stays your file: edits are done locally and .docx, .pptx, .xlsx, and .md and synced to the cloud after
- every change is reviewable: edits show up as tracked diffs that you accept or reject, at the smallest unit that makes sense (e.g. a sentence in .docx)
- free, and no new subscription needed: bring whichever AI plan or plans you already have. You shouldn't have to pay twice for the same inference, and you SHOULD take advantage of the insane subsidization in the current ChatGPT and Claude plans. 
- Bots with any AI: I love the concept of grok bot, not so much its limited choice of models. I strongly believe that long-standing "ai teammates" should be agent neutral and in your controlTry mimzie out: it's a free beta at mimzie.comit's early, lots of rough edges, but I've had the time of my life developing it.I'd love to answer questions and hear any and all feedback.

body:
# OddlyGoods/peep-note

Save and recall useful LLM responses, Markdown notes, and screenshots.

## Languages

- JavaScript
- Shell
- TypeScript

## Top Contributors

- chYoo01 (263 contributions)

---

## README

# PeepNote

PeepNote is a local-first desktop app for saving useful LLM responses, recording your own thoughts, and finding them again while you work. Keep Markdown answers and screenshots together, recall them with a shortcut, and organize related records into AI summaries.

> PeepNote keeps its application data on the local computer. AI summaries are optional and require an API key configured by the user.

## News

- **2026-11-09 — v1.3.0** — Added Map, recently viewed Quick List ordering, and Alt+X to toggle global shortcuts.
- **2026-11-05 — v1.2.0** — Added Magic Pen and data folder switching.
- **2026-11-03 — v1.1.8** — Added remote connection guides, configurable context length, and automatic batched AI summaries.
- **2026-11-03 — v1.1.7** — Fixed Linux update errors and added HTTP API endpoint support.
- **2026-10-30 — v1.1.5** — Added MCP support, save notifications, and AI connection testing.

## See it in action

### 1. Save LLM responses as Markdown notes

Keep the answers worth revisiting without searching through a long conversation. Copy an LLM response, press `Alt+1`, choose **Markdown**, and paste it into a note. Save with `Ctrl+Enter`, then open the note to review its headings, tables, and code blocks.

Copy an LLM response, save it as a Markdown note, and review the saved content

### 2. Capture diagrams and screenshots

Save the visual parts of an answer alongside your notes. Press `Alt+2`, drag to select a screen region, and capture a diagram, code example, or reference image. Open the saved screenshot to inspect the details.

Select a screen region and review the saved diagram in PeepNote

### 3. Recall notes with Quick List

Bring saved answers back into your workflow without searching through the main window. Press `Alt+Q` to open Quick List and move to the next item; use `Alt+E` to go back. Open an item when you need its full content. Quick List uses the currently selected date range.

Browse saved notes and screenshots with Quick List, then open a record

### 4. Turn related notes into an AI summary

Bring answers from multiple LLM conversations together. Use **Manage** to select related records, create a group, and click **AI Summary** to organize the material into one structured note. Summaries use the provider and API key configured in **Settings → AI settings**. Response language defaults to your PeepNote language; choose a specific language to use it for both summaries and Magic Pen replies. AI settings, Magic Pen and MCP each have their own **Save** button.

Group related RAG notes and generate a structured AI summary

### 5. Keep note previews private with Secret

Enable **Secret** when creating a note to hide its content in list previews. Opening the saved note prompts for your four-digit PIN before showing its contents. Set your PIN in **Settings → Secret note lock**.

Create a note with Secret enabled, then open it to see the PIN prompt

### 6. Explore screen content with Magic Pen

Press `Alt+S` and draw around text, a diagram, or anything you want to understand on your screen. Magic Pen explains the selected content in a movable response window. Ask follow-up questions by typing or selecting another area, then save the conversation as a Markdown note in your chosen workspace. Choose your AI API or an installed, signed-in AI tool in **Settings → AI settings → Magic Pen**.

Select content with Magic Pen, ask a follow-up question, and save the conversation as a note

## Configuration

PeepNote opens directly to the main screen. There are no app accounts, login forms, Google sign-in, session tokens or authentication server. All windows use one local data space for notes, workspaces, settings and optional AI keys. OS user accounts still have their own application data directories.

The optional `VITE_LOCAL_SERVER_PORT` setting in `.env.example` defaults to `3848`, separate from the original PeepNote app. It is read at build time. The API listens only on `127.0.0.1` and rejects unrelated browser origins and hosts. No API key is bundled: enter your own provider key in Settings only if you use AI summaries.

The package and Linux executable are named `peep-note`. The app keeps its existing `open-peep-note` data directory and internal application ID so installed copies continue to read the same notes and settings after updates.

## Features

- Create text, Markdown, code, and HTML notes
- Capture a selected screen region and record a selected screen region
- Draw directly over the live screen with `Alt+S` to ask AI about a selected area. In **Settings → AI settings → Magic Pen**, choose **AI API** to use the provider and API key from AI settings, or **AI tools** to choose Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, or Qwen Code (the selected CLI must be installed and signed in). Magic Pen remembers its own model and custom input for each provider and tool, separately from summaries. API models must support image input. A movable response window shows the provider, model and duration, supports follow-up questions and captures, and saves the conversation with its images as a Markdown note. The window closes after a successful save. Codex analysis does not save a Codex session; change or disable the shortcut in **Settings → Global shortcuts**.
- Select and remember a preferred monitor for capture and recording
- Organize records with workspaces, tags, date ranges, search, and groups
- Restore deleted records from Trash during a configurable retention period (7, 10, 30, or 90 days; default 10), or permanently delete them. Individually deleted AI summaries are removed immediately; deleting a whole group keeps its summary in Trash with the group.
- Search Korean and English text in screenshots and attached images using local OCR
- Generate AI summaries with OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, or Qwen
- Connect Codex and other MCP clients to search, save, edit and group non-secret notes
- Use global shortcuts and a recent-record Quick List
- Protect secret notes with a four-digit PIN and masked list previews
- English, Korean, Japanese, and Simplified Chinese UI
- Light and dark themes

## Requirements

### Development environment

- Node.js 20 or newer
- npm 10 or newer
- Windows 10/11 or a current Linux distribution
- Build installers on the target operating system when possible: Windows for `.exe`, Linux for `.deb`

For Ubuntu 22.04 or newer, install Electron runtime dependencies:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y build-essential libnss3 libatk1.0-0 libatk-bridge2.0-0 \
  libcups2 libdrm2 libgtk-3-0 libgbm1 libasound2t64 libxss1 \
  xdg-utils xdg-desktop-portal xdg-desktop-portal-gtk
```

On Ubuntu 22.04, the audio package can be named `libasound2` instead of `libasound2t64`.

Wayland screen capture relies on PipeWire and an xdg-desktop-portal implementation for your desktop environment. Some Wayland compositors restrict global shortcuts; an Xorg session is the fallback if a shortcut cannot be registered.

## Install and run

### Development

```bash
git clone https://github.com/OddlyGoods/peep-note.git
cd peep-note
npm ci --onnxruntime-node-install-cuda=skip
npm run dev
```

Stop the development process with `Ctrl+C`. If the app remains in the system tray, use **Quit** from the tray menu to terminate the Electron process completely.

### Linux package

Build a Debian package:

```bash
npm run build:linux
```

The package is written to `release/`:

```bash
sudo apt install ./release/PeepNote-*-linux-amd64.deb
```

To produce an unpacked build for a quick smoke test:

```bash
npm run build:linux:dir
./release/linux-unpacked/peep-note
```

To update an existing PeepNote installation manually, install a newer `.deb` with the same command. Existing local records and settings are preserved.

### Windows package

Build the Windows installer on Windows:

```powershell
npm run build:win
```

The NSIS installer is written to `release/`. Run the generated `PeepNote-*-Setup.exe` and choose the normal install flow. Running the installer again updates an existing installation while preserving local records and settings.

Windows supports the same core features as Linux, including notes, local storage, comments, themes, AI summaries, capture, recording, tray controls, and global shortcuts. Capture behavior, multi-monitor DPI scaling, and shortcut availability should still be smoke-tested on the target Windows setup.

## Build commands

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run dev` | Run the development Electron app with Vite. |
| `npm run build` | Build using electron-builder's default target. |
| `npm run build:linux` | Build the Linux x64 Debian package. |
| `npm run build:linux:dir` | Build an unpacked Linux x64 app in `release/linux-unpacked/`. |
| `npm run build:win` | Build the Windows NSIS installer. |
| `npm run release` | Create a release build and publish through the configured electron-builder provider. |
| `npm run test:updates` | Test update state, retries, renderer recovery, installation and release validation without installing anything. |
| `npm run verify:release` | Check the package/lockfile version and optional `RELEASE_TAG`. |

## App updates

Installed Windows and Ubuntu `.deb` builds check for updates automatically. To check manually, go to **Settings → App information → App updates → Check for updates**.

Choose **Download**, then **Restart and install** when you are ready. Ubuntu may ask for administrator authentication. Notes, attachments, and settings are preserved. Development and unpacked builds do not support in-app updates.

## Usage guide

### Date navigation

In **Settings → General**, **Automatically advance dates** updates the main list's end date to today when you reopen or refocus the app. By default, the start date moves with it to preserve the selected range length. Enable the separate **Fix start date** option to keep the selected start date and advance only the end date. Both options are saved independently; with automatic advancement off, the selected dates remain unchanged. You can still change dates manually. The separate Search screen uses its own date range.

### Trash

**Trash** is in the left navigation, below **Favorites**. Deleting a record, selected records, or a group moves its records to Trash and removes them from normal lists, search, Quick List, and calendar counts. Deleted groups appear as a single group, including their AI summary, and can be restored or permanently deleted together. Select records to restore them or permanently delete them. **Empty** permanently deletes all of the current user's trashed records after confirmation.

### Image text search

Open an image record and click **Extract text** to recognize its screenshot or attached images. Saving, opening, editing, restoring records, and launching the app never start extraction automatically. Interrupted requests must be started again. Korean and English recognition models ship with the app; OCR runs locally without an AI API key or uploading images. The first extraction prepares local models under the app's data directory. Extraction may take time for large images. Images larger than 40 MB are skipped; recognition accuracy depends on image quality and typography. Use **Search** to find previously extracted image text alongside titles and note contents.

### Create a record

1. Click **Add**, or open the quick composer with `Alt+1`.
2. Choose **Note**, **Capture**, or **Video**.
3. For notes, choose Text, Markdown, Code, or HTML.
4. Add an optional title, content, tags, and workspace, then save.

When adding files, choose **Link original files** to save space or **Copy to PeepNote** to keep an independent copy. Each attachment shows its mode. Linked originals are never deleted by PeepNote; moving or deleting them breaks the link.

For screenshots and recordings, choose a region after selecting the capture action. Use the adjustment button next to the capture/record control in the main composer to choose a different monitor; PeepNote remembers the selected monitor for later captures.

### Default global shortcuts

| Shortcut | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `Alt+W` | Open or hide the main window |
| `Alt+F` | Open the favorites list; hide the focused main window if the list is already open |
| `Alt+1` | Open the quick composer |
| `Alt+2` | Capture a screenshot region |
| `Alt+3` | Start screen recording |
| `Alt+4` | Stop screen recording |
| `Alt+Q` | Open the Quick List / move to the next item while it is open |
| `Alt+E` | Move to the previous Quick List item |

Shortcuts can be changed in **Settings → Global shortcuts**.
Use the **⋯** menu beside a shortcut to disable or re-enable it while keeping its key combination. Click **Save** to apply your changes.

### Secret notes

Enable the **Secret** badge while creating or editing a note to mask its preview in lists. Set a four-digit secret PIN in **Settings → Secret note lock**. Opening a secret note requests the PIN; after a successful entry, secret notes remain unlocked for one minute in the current app session.

The PIN is stored as a hash, not plain text. A four-digit PIN is a convenience lock, not full-disk encryption; use operating-system account protection for highly sensitive data.

### MCP connection

PeepNote provides a local **Streamable HTTP** MCP server. No separate Node.js installation or cloud backend is needed for an installed app. Keep PeepNote running; it can remain in the tray.

1. Open **Settings → AI settings → MCP** and turn on **Allow MCP connections**. It is off by default. Click **Save** at the bottom of the MCP card to apply your changes.
2. Select **Codex**, **Claude Code**, or **Gemini CLI** to see its connection instructions.
3. For Codex, click **Copy configuration**, add the block to `~/.codex/config.toml`, and fully restart Codex. For Claude Code or Gemini CLI, click **Copy command**, run it in your terminal, and restart that client. The command registers PeepNote for your user account. Check the connection with `/mcp` in Claude Code or `/mcp list` in Gemini CLI.
4. Ask your client to “Find my RAG notes” or “Save this answer in PeepNote as Markdown.”

The copied content includes the local server URL (normally `http://127.0.0.1:3848/mcp`) and its authorization header. The Claude and Gemini options are for **Claude Code** and **Gemini CLI**, rather than their web chat apps. For other clients, use **Streamable HTTP** with the displayed URL and private header.

The connection configuration contains a dedicated MCP token, separate from AI provider API keys. Do not publish or share it. Saving MCP as disabled blocks access; enabling it again and saving generates a new token, so copy the configuration again. A custom local API port is reflected in the copied URL. Remote computers and cloud sessions cannot reach this loopback-only endpoint without a separate connection setup.

Available tools: `search_notes`, `get_note`, `create_note`, `update_note` (replace or append), `set_favorite`, `list_workspaces`, `create_workspace`, `list_groups`, `create_group`, `trash_notes`, and `trash_group`.

- Secret notes are excluded from search, results, counts and direct access. MCP cannot create, unlock, modify or delete them. Groups containing active secret notes cannot be deleted through MCP.
- No settings, provider API keys, password hashes, attachment paths, file-reading tools, AI provider calls or permanent-deletion tools are exposed.
- MCP deletion always moves records to Trash, including individually deleted AI summaries. Normal Trash retention and automatic expiry still apply. Whole groups and their summaries can be restored together in the app.
- Creating groups requires ungrouped, non-secret notes from the same workspace. MCP changes refresh the app's lists; an open edit draft is preserved.
- Notes returned to an MCP client may be sent to that client's AI model. Stored note text is data, not instructions for the client to execute.

Run `npm run test:mcp` for protocol, authentication, secret-note exclusion, write and recovery tests. These use a real MCP client over loopback HTTP with a temporary database, not your notes.

### AI summaries

1. Open **Settings → AI settings**.
2. Select a provider and model, then enter your API key.
3. Create a group from selected records and press **AI Summary**.

Summary titles and content use the app language selected in Settings, regardless of the language of the original records. Code, commands, URLs, and identifiers retain their original form.

Secret note content is excluded from AI summaries. Video files are not uploaded for summaries; only relevant written record content is used.

## Data and privacy

Notes, attachments, and settings are stored on your computer. AI summaries are optional; using them sends the selected non-secret written content to the provider configured in Settings with your own API key. Image text extraction runs locally.

Application data is stored locally. Typical locations are:

```text
Linux:   ~/.config/open-peep-note
Windows: %APPDATA%/open-peep-note
```

The legacy directory name is retained for compatibility. It contains the local database, screenshots, recordings, and application settings. Back up this directory before reinstalling the operating system or moving to another computer.

To choose a different data folder, open **Settings → App information → Data location → Change folder**. Select an empty folder, save any unfinished notes and settings, then confirm **Copy and restart**. PeepNote copies your records, managed media, OCR models, and settings and updates stored attachment paths before opening the new location. Original files are kept as a backup. Keep the selected drive available whenever you use the app.

## License

PeepNote is released under the Apache License 2.0.

What is FilmCraft?
FilmCraft is a next-generation non-linear video editing system (NLE) engineered from the ground up in systems Rust, designed specifically to address the stability, bloat, and recurring cost issues of proprietary commercial editors. Built originally by the ArtCraft open-source collective and actively maintained under the GNU General Public License v3.0 (GPLv3), FilmCraft runs completely offline with zero telemetry, zero mandatory cloud account logins, and zero subscription fees.
Unlike legacy free editors that force non-standard timeline paradigms, FilmCraft deliberately implements the industry-standard track patching, 3-point ripple editing, multi-cam sync, and dual-monitor layout familiar to professional Adobe Premiere Pro and DaVinci Resolve editors. By adopting native GPU rendering via Apple Metal, NVIDIA CUDA/NVENC, and Vulkan/VA-API, FilmCraft delivers instantaneous 4K 10-bit ProRes and H.265 playback with sub-500MB idle memory consumption.

title: Show HN: PDFMeasure – Measure PDF files in the browser
author: fra
body: Hi HN, sharing a little app I built to measure architectural drawings in the browser. My architects on a remodel had this fancy software to do it, but I was frustrated to not be able to do the same easily.It does much of what the more complex software does: measure distance, surface areas, perimeters, angles; markup; takeoff (count & run lengths), ...etc. I even built an overlay feature to compare two pages.In this age of AI, I think simple software such as this can only ever be free. How do you offer a web app for free? Make it local only. I think there is a lot of space to explore in local-first web apps.

body:
# README.md

- Branch: main
- Repository: Dr-Logvinovich/codon-torus-syntax

---

# From Form to Program & The Double-Stranded Codon Torus ($\mathbb{T}_4^3 = (\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z})^3$): Conditional Codon Syntax, Markovian Lumpability & Synthetic mRNA Forensics

Codon Torus & Syntax CI
Zenodo Preprint I (v14.8)
Zenodo Preprint II (Torus v3.5)
ORCID: V. Logvinovich
ORCID: J.-C. Perez
Offline Cache Included
Python 3.9+
License: MIT

> **Official Open-Science Verification Repository for the Genomic Information Theory & Double-Stranded Codon Torus Research Programme (Complete with 568 MB Pre-Cached NCBI RefSeq/GenBank Archives, Zero-RNG Proofs & Pre-Computed Audit Reports).**
>
> * **Authors:** **Victor Logvinovich** (Master of Physical and Mathematical Sciences; Researcher in Pedagogical Sciences (Mathematics), Kobrin, Belarus; ORCID: 0009-0007-2040-6955) and **Jean-Claude Perez** (PhD in Mathematics and Computer Science, Retired IBM AI European Research Centre, Montpellier; Luc Montagnier Foundation; ORCID: 0000-0001-6446-2042).
> * ** Zenodo Preprint I (`v14.8`):** https://zenodo.org/records/23479667
> * **Zenodo Preprint II (`v3.5`):** https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23508080

---

## Complete Repository Architecture (100% Self-Contained & Offline-Ready)

Unlike standard bioinformatics repositories that require hours of external FTP downloads before a single test can run, this repository includes the **entire 568 MB local NCBI cache (`cds_cache/`, 103 SHA-256 verified genomic files)** and **all pre-computed verification outputs (`results_verified/`)**:

| Path / Artifact | Category | Contents & Verification Scope |
| :--- | :---: | :--- |
| **`code_logos_perez_v14_8.tex.pdf`** | **Preprint I (34 pp.)** | *"From Form to Program: Medium-Range Conditional Codon Syntax Inside Real Genes — Strict Null-Model Evidence Across 54 Cellular RefSeq Taxa, a Codon-Mirror-Symmetry Control, Two-Scale Phylogenetic Transfer, Intron-Exon Compartment Confinement, Synthetic Genome Forensics, and the Biotech 'Max-CAI' Codon-Optimization Crash"* (`v14.8`). |
| **`codon_torus_logos_perez_v3.tex.pdf`** | **Preprint II (33 pp.)** | *"The Double-Stranded Codon Torus: Duplex Mirror Fibration of DNA Coding Space, Markovian Lumpability, and Information-Theoretic Consequences"* (`v3.5`). |
| **`super_codon_proof_v14_8.py`** | **Verification Engine I** | Autonomous self-testing pipeline (`v14.6–v14.8`): 10-level null model hierarchy (`H0`–`H7`) across 54 cellular RefSeq taxa + SARS-CoV-2, 14-gene human RefSeqGene intron-exon compartment confinement (`TP53`, `KRAS`, `BRCA1`, etc.), 13 frontier genomes (Giant Viruses, 2.8 km boreholes, $122^\circ\text{C}$ archaea, Venter's `JCVI-syn1.0` & `JCVI-syn3.0`), viral "Genetic Trojans" (`HPV-16 E7`, `Adenovirus E3 RID-\alpha`), organelle OS rewriting, and the `Max-CAI` crash test. |

For decades, synthetic biology and industrial mRNA design have relied on a zero-order assumption: if you replace every sense codon with its single "most frequent" human synonym (the **Max-CAI / Max-GC3** standard), the amino-acid sequence on paper remains 100% identical, so translation should only improve.

title: Show HN: Movement breaks that only show up while Claude Code is working
author: imohammadreza
body:
# mamrezme/30yr-uptime

A Claude Code mod that turns the time you wait on Claude into short movement breaks: neck, back, hips, wrists, eyes, acted out by a pixel character. Local only, no tokens.

- Stars: 1
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 1
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-11-08T20:06:58Z

## Languages

- Python
- TypeScript

## Topics

- break-reminder
- claude-code
- claude-code-mod
- claude-code-mods
- claude-code-plugin
- ergonomics
- terminal
- wellness

## Top Contributors

- mamrezme (1 contributions)

---

## README

# 30yr-uptime

A Claude Code mod that turns the time you spend waiting on Claude into short movement breaks. Every 45 minutes, the next time a turn runs longer than 15 seconds, a break shows above the prompt: something for your neck, shoulders, back, hips, legs, wrists, eyes or lungs, acted out by a little pixel character. Press **Done**, **In 5 min** or **Skip**. It all happens in the terminal and runs locally: no network, no model calls, no tokens.

A break showing up while Claude works, then /break

> **Chin tucks** 10 reps: slide your head straight back, hold for 2 seconds. Resets your neck over your spine. Skip it and your head keeps drifting toward the monitor.

The character is an unofficial fan take on Clawd, Claude Code's character; this mod is not made or endorsed by Anthropic.

## The moves

The character acting out each break above the spinner while Claude works

| Move | Setting key | What it is for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stand up | `stand` | Getting out of the chair |
| Drink water | `water` | Hydration |
| Walk | `walk` | Circulation |
| Eye rest (20-20-20) | `eyes` | Eye strain: 20 feet away for 20 seconds |
| Box breathing | `breathe` | In 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4, three rounds |
| Chin tucks | `neck` | Forward head posture |
| Shoulder blade squeeze | `shoulders` | Rounded shoulders |
| Chair back extension | `thoracic` | Hunching (upper back) |
| Seated twist | `twist` | Spine rotation, 15 seconds each side |
| Wrist stretches | `wrists` | Forearms and wrists, both hands, fingers up and down |
| Squats | `squat` | Glutes and thighs |
| Lunges | `lunge` | Legs, one at a time, and the front of the hips |
| Glute kickbacks | `glutes` | Weak glutes, 10 each side |
| Hamstring stretch | `hamstring` | Tight backs of the thighs, 20 seconds each leg |
| Calf stretch | `calf` | Tight calves and ankles, 20 seconds each leg |
| Hip flexor stretch | `hipflexor` | Hips that sitting keeps folded, 20 seconds each side |

All of them are done standing or sitting next to the desk, with no equipment.

Each move is animated and framed on the part of the body it works (chin tucks are a close-up of the head and neck), with reps counted, holds counted down and a progress bar. Breaks are picked at random from the moves you have on, one at a time, never the same move twice in a row. Terminals narrower than 54 columns get words and buttons only, and `NO_COLOR` is respected.

All sixteen breaks, four frames each

## Install

```
/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/mamrezme/30yr-uptime.git
/plugin install 30yr-uptime@30yr-uptime
```

Then `/reload-plugins` (or restart Claude Code). The HTTPS link works with or without SSH keys for GitHub; the short form `mamrezme/30yr-uptime` may try SSH first. Or run it from a clone without installing:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/mamrezme/30yr-uptime.git
claude --plugin-dir ./30yr-uptime
```

To update: `/plugin marketplace update 30yr-uptime`, then `/plugin update 30yr-uptime@30yr-uptime`. To remove it: `/plugin uninstall 30yr-uptime@30yr-uptime`.

Needs Claude Code 2.1.287 or newer (mods are on by default from there); tested on 2.1.319. The animation needs a terminal at least 54 columns wide; narrower, the break shows as words and buttons only.

## The `/break` command

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/break` | Starts a break now, with its animation: a random move among the ones you have on. If a break is already on show, it stays and the command says so. |
| `/break off` | Turns the reminders off, in this session and the next ones, until `/break on`. A snoozed break is dropped. `/break` still starts a break when you ask for one. |
| `/break on` | Turns the reminders back on. The wait starts over from that moment, so no reminder shows straight away. |
| `/break config` | Lists the settings as they apply now. |
| `/break moves` | Lists every move, its key, and whether it is on. |
| `/break set ` | Changes a setting, e.g. `/break set waitSeconds 30` or `/break set squat off`. |
| `/break reset [key]` | Puts one setting back to its default, or all of them with no key. |

`/break` runs at once, even while Claude is working. The mod's store holds only whether reminders are off and the settings you changed; Done, Skip and In 5 min keep no record.

## Settings

Installing asks nothing: every setting has a default and the mod works as it is. To change one, use `/break set` (see the `/break` command); it applies at once and is kept for later sessions.

| Setting | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `waitSeconds` | 15 | How long a turn must run before a break is suggested. 1 to 3600. |
| `intervalMinutes` | 45 | The shortest time between two breaks, counted from the session start for the first one: a break waits until this long has passed and a turn runs past `waitSeconds`. Never while Claude is idle. 1 to 1440; 0 gives every long turn a break. |
| one key per move (see the moves) | on | Whether that move can be suggested. |

Turn off the moves you can't or don't want to do (`/break set squat off`); with every move off, no breaks are shown. `/break set` refuses a value that is not a number (or a negative one) and a move value other than on or off (`on`/`off`, `true`/`false`, `yes`/`no`, `1`/`0`), and clamps a number to its range. Changing a setting keeps the break on show and a snoozed one.

The settings are not in `/config`: Claude Code counts every `/config` option of a plugin as "not yet set" after install, even one with a default, and asks you to configure it.

## What the hooks do

`hooks/register.tsx` hooks six events. It reads them and draws; it never changes what Claude sees or sends:

- `session.start`: reads whether you turned reminders off and the settings you changed, checks `NO_COLOR`, registers `/break`, and in an interactive session starts a 5-second timer that decides when a break is due.
- `command.run` for `/break`: starts a break now, turns the reminders off or on, or shows and changes the settings, and remembers those choices.
- `turn.start`: notes when Claude's main turn began, so a long turn can be spotted (a subagent's turn doesn't count).
- `turn.complete`: notes that the main turn ended and takes the scene off the spinner.
- `ui.render` on `Spinner`: while a break is on show and Claude works, draws its scene above the spinner line and leaves the spinner as it is. Below 54 columns, or outside the terminal, it hands the spinner back unchanged.
- `ui.render` on `AbovePrompt`: shows the break's words and the Done, In 5 min and Skip buttons, with the scene above them while Claude is idle.

While a scene is on screen, a timer repaints it about 12 times a second; it stops as soon as the break is answered.

## Privacy: what data it sends

None. The mod makes no network requests and no model calls, so it uses none of your tokens. It doesn't read your prompts, Claude's replies, your files or your code: it only sees when a turn starts and ends, the terminal size, and `NO_COLOR`. Every line of text is written into the mod; none is generated. It stores two things in Claude Code's own plugin store: whether you ran `/break off` (`paused`) and the settings you changed with `/break set` (`settings`). It keeps no record of the breaks you took or skipped. There is no server, so there is no privacy policy to link.

title: Show HN: Aisync, advisory file claims so two AI agents don't edit one repo
author: MaxTigerYoung
body:
GitHub - MaxonT/aisync: aisync — AGENTS.md, but for live coordination between AI tools. One standup for all your AI coding tools: shared rules, a hash-chained journal, file claims and mid-session news for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. · GitHub

## Folders and files

| Name | Name | Last commit message | Last commit date |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| .github | .github | | |
| .trace | .trace | | |
| ai_sync | ai_sync | | |
| docs | docs | | |
| tests | tests | | |
| tools | tools | | |
| .DS_Store | .DS_Store | | |
| .gitignore | .gitignore | | |
| Dockerfile | Dockerfile | | |
| LICENSE | LICENSE | | |
| README.md | README.md | | |
| README.zh-CN.md | README.zh-CN.md | | |
| pyproject.toml | pyproject.toml | | |
| View all files | | | |

# aisync: one standup for all your AI coding agents

Claude Code, Codex and Cursor share rules, a journal and file claims, and hear what the others did mid-session.

 

English · 中文 · Website · Demo status board

Note

Your AI tools are coworkers who never talk. aisync is their standup. Every tool works out of one local hub (`~/.ai-sync/`, a git repo). Before editing, an agent claims files, and an overlapping claim exits with code 3, so the agent stops before it collides. Every decision, blocker and commit goes into one hash-chained journal. Hooks tell a running Claude Code, Codex or Cursor session what the other tools just did, and stay silent when nothing changed.

If aisync keeps your agents from stepping on each other, a star helps other people find it.

## Install

Give it to your AI. It reads the page, does a dry run first and asks before it changes anything:

```
Read https://maxont.github.io/aisync/install and install aisync for me.

```

Or in a terminal. It installs with uv, pipx or pip and never edits your shell config:

```
curl -fsSL https://maxont.github.io/aisync/install.sh | bash
```

Needs Python 3.11+ and git, on macOS or Linux. Nothing else: aisync uses only the standard library.

After your first successful command, the CLI asks once: `Star MaxonT/aisync on GitHub? [y/N]`. The default is no, it never asks again, and it stays silent in CI, pipes and scripts. A yes stars the repo through your own `gh` login (or prints the link if `gh` is missing). Set `NO_STAR_PROMPT=1` to skip the question.

## See it

 A real terminal run: `aisync demo` (synthetic data), then two tools reach for the same file. Step by step: how it works · the same demo hub as a status board. 

| | Rules sync tools | aisync |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claims | None: two agents can edit the same file at once | `aisync claim` first; an overlap exits with code 3 and says who holds the files |
| Journal | No shared record of who did what | One append-only, hash-chained log of commits, decisions and blockers (`aisync verify`) |
| Mid-session news | Rules load when a session starts, then go quiet | Hooks inject what the other tools just did into the running session |

aisync also does the rules part: one rules block copied into every tool's own rule file, synced 3-way, conflicts never overwritten.

Dogfooded: 6,700+ journal events from 7 AI tools over 4 weeks.

## Use it

```
aisync demo            # a throwaway hub with a synthetic two-week journal
aisync init            # create ~/.ai-sync (or wherever AISYNC_HOME points)
aisync install-hooks   # shows every tool config change as a diff, then asks
aisync watch &         # event-driven sync loop (or run `aisync sync` by hand)
```

What an agent does during a session:

```
aisync claim   -a codex -p api -f app/payments/ -m "SDK upgrade"  # 3 = taken
aisync log     -a codex -p api -m "SDK 5.0, retries kept"
aisync rule add -a codex --when "changing an API" --do "add a contract test"
aisync release -a codex -p api
```

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `init` | create the hub: shared rules, journal, config, local git repo |
| `log` | append one event (`dev_log`, `decision`, `blocked`, `unblocked`, `rule_change`, `note`) |
| `rule add` / `rule list` | any agent adds a shared rule (`--when/--do/--not`, `--topic`, `--replaces R-012`); every tool's copy gets it on the next sync |
| `rule lint` / `rule rewrite` / `rule enforcement` | rules not in the When/Do/Not shape / rewrite them by ID without losing a fact / which test or hook keeps each rule |
| `tidy` | rules clerk: likely duplicates, rules nobody cited lately, core layer over budget; proposals only, you tick them |
| `rulecheck` | prove a rules cleanup lost no hard fact (paths, numbers, commands, IDs) |
| `instinct` | optional habit list grown from past mistakes, injected into every session |
| `mcp` | serve the hub to any MCP agent over stdio (`pip install 'aisync[mcp]'`) |
| `claim` / `release` / `claims` | who is working on which files right now; overlap = exit 3 |
| `news` | what other tools did since this session last looked |
| `hook ` | entry point for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor hooks (reads hook JSON, never fails) |
| `install-hooks` | wire the hooks, seed the rules block, add the git `Agent:` trailer hook; diff first, asks before writing (`--dry-run`, `--yes`) |
| `status` | health, conflicts, claims, blockers, metrics (exit 1 when something needs you) |
| `board` | write the hub as one static HTML page: claims, blockers, who did what, timeline |
| `report` | read-only self-check: silent tools, commits without an `Agent:` trailer, stale blockers |
| `tail` | latest journal events |
| `verify` | check the hash chain |
| `sync` / `watch` | run one sync cycle / the debounced, event-driven loop |
| `resolve` / `resume` | rule on a rule conflict / clear failure counters after a pause |
| `demo` | the throwaway hub shown above |

## New in 0.2.0: rules as interfaces, loaded in layers

A rules file grows until every session pays for it and nobody reads it. 0.2.0 treats a rule like an API:

- When / Do / Not. Each rule is one line with a stable ID: `[R-087] When:. Do:. Not:.` The why goes to the journal, not the rule. `rule_spec = true` refuses anything else; `rule lint` lists misfits; `rule rewrite` reshapes old rules by ID and refuses a rewrite that drops a path, number or command.
- Layers. Mark a tool copy `layer = "core"`: it carries `core_topics` in full and every other topic as one line. When a prompt or tool call touches a topic's keywords (`[shelf]`), the hook injects that topic once per session. On the author's own hub this cut the always-loaded rules from 20,673 to 7,876 tokens; replaying 7 days of transcripts, 98.9% of the 189 times a folded rule was cited, it had been injected before the citation.
- A stable prefix.`progress_file` moves the live progress table out of the shared page, so the page stays byte-identical and prompt caches keep hitting: the next session after a journal event read 61,151 cached tokens instead of 13,060.
- A clerk, not a janitor.`aisync tidy` proposes (duplicates, uncited rules, budget overruns) and never edits; a replaced rule moves to `rules-archive.md` with its ID, nothing is deleted.
- Any agent. Three doors: the AGENTS.md page, the CLI, and `aisync mcp` (tools: rules, rule_add, log, claim, release, news, status, tidy). The core stays standard-library only; the MCP SDK is the optional `aisync[mcp]` extra.

## How it works

 Step through it at your own pace (play, pause, ← →) 

A sync cycle is `harvest` (new git commits in watched repos become journal events, attributed by their `Agent:` trailer) → `rules` (new entries in repos you list in `rule_sources`) → `distribute` (3-way sync of the rules block into each tool file) → `render` (progress page) → `flush` (commit the hub, optional push). Each step is isolated: one failure never blocks the others.

The rules block is synced 3-way. If only the truth changed, copies are overwritten (with a backup). If one copy was edited and nobody else changed anything, the edit is adopted everywhere. If both sides changed, nothing is overwritten: it becomes a conflict for you to resolve.

Reliability and observability: timeouts and retries with backoff on every git call, failure isolation per step and per project, auto-pause after `fail_threshold` failures in a row with an `ALERT.md` and a desktop notification, a per-cycle run log (`state/runs.jsonl`), hook call stats and `aisync status` for all of it.

## Configuration

`~/.ai-sync/config.toml` (set `AISYNC_HOME` to put the hub anywhere):

```
roster = ["claude-code", "codex", "cursor"]   # tools `report` expects to hear from
scan_dirs = ["~/projects"]                    # every git repo inside is watched
rule_sources = []                             # repos whose AGENTS.md "## Meta rule" feeds shared rules
remote = ""                                   # e.g. "origin" to also push the hub

progress_file = "progress.md"                 # keep agents.md byte-stable; hooks inject progress at session start
rule_spec = true                              # rule add only accepts When/Do/Not rules
require_enforcer = false                      # true: every new rule names --enforced-by or --judgment-only
core_topics = ["Safety", "Meta"]              # topic headings a layered copy carries in full
instincts_path = ""                           # optional habit file injected at session start
tidy_daily = false                            # the watcher starts one `aisync tidy --write` a day
tidy_usage_globs = []                         # files whose R-### mentions count as a rule being used

[shelf]                                       # folded topic -> keywords that pull it into a session
Deploys = ["deploy", "terraform", "rollback"]

[[target]]                                    # files carrying the shared-rules block
label = "claude-code"
path = "~/.claude/CLAUDE.md"
layer = "core"                                # optional: fold non-core topics, inject them on demand
```

To keep `aisync watch` running, start it from your login items, a systemd user unit or a launchd agent that runs `aisync watch`; create `~/.ai-sync/STOP` to stop it cleanly.

## Standing on the shoulders of

> aisync: AGENTS.md, but for live coordination between AI tools.

| Project | How it shaped aisync |
| --- | --- |
| | The starting idea: one plain-text instruction file every agent reads, no SDK. aisync keeps that shape for shared rules (one rules block copied into each tool's own AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md) and adds what a static file cannot say: who is editing what right now, and what changed since the session started. |
| | Mid-session news rides on Claude Code hooks: `aisync install-hooks` adds SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit and PostToolUse entries to ~/.claude/settings.json, and `aisync hook claude-code` answers with hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext only when another tool changed something. |
| | Codex reads ~/.codex/AGENTS.md, which is where aisync seeds the shared rules block, and its hooks.json takes the same SessionStart / UserPromptSubmit / PostToolUse events, so `aisync hook codex` reuses the Claude Code reply format. |
| Cursor | Cursor hooks (~/.cursor/hooks.json) deliver the rules and progress at sessionStart and the news after each postToolUse through additional_context, because Cursor's User Rules live inside the app instead of a file aisync could sync. |
| | The journal borrows git's hash chain: every event stores the id of the one before it and its own id is a SHA-256 of that link plus its body, so `aisync verify` spots any edited, lost or reordered line. The hub itself is a local git repo. |

aisync is an independent project, not affiliated with the projects above.

## Development

```
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests   # includes wheel -> venv -> demo
```

The images are generated: the terminal GIF is a recorded real run of `.github/refine/demo-terminal.json`, the how-it-works animation comes from `.github/refine/how-it-works.stages.json`, and the credits above from `.github/refine/lineage.json`. All demo data is synthetic.

MIT licensed.

aisync — AGENTS.md, but for live coordination between AI tools. One standup for all your AI coding tools: shared rules, a hash-chained journal, file claims and mid-session news for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor.

author: shanjv05
body: Cloakroom is an open-source privacy tool that masks secrets and sensitive data from AI agents. It swaps real values for placeholders, then swaps them back to the originals locally.I was trying to build a full on local LLM setup on my machine, but the local models were not up to the mark (at least, not yet). I ended up building a hybrid setup, with the cloud for planning and local models for execution. I realized I needed a privacy layer so cloud models could not access sensitive data, and I built Cloakroom.It runs on your machine, it’s cross-platform, and it works with Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex CLI.

title: Show HN: Zeus – Claude Code for AI voice agents
author: kolchinski
body:
Hey, Alex here, I'm one of the founders. We've built phone agents for enterprise customers for two years and kept seeing the same failure: agents that mishear callers and then do something confidently wrong.We're announcing two things in this launch. #1 is the stack: 
instead of one transcription model → one LLM → one TTS, most conversation turns runs through several transcription models and LLMs (a fast and a slow LLM in the same call, models switched per turn, audio sent straight to an LLM alongside transcripts). That gets us 99.4% on Big Bench Audio. That's the second-highest published score; the only model above us takes almost 9 seconds to start talking as far as we've measured, which doesn't work on a phone call. Eval set and transcripts are on Hugging Face - http://huggingface.co/datasets/kolchinski/bba-storm-eval#2 is Zeus, an agent that configures our voice AI stack per use case and per conversation. We tried doing this with Claude Code and Codex and they were bad at it: they can't run simulated calls out of the box, don't do well with audio input and spotting problems in calls, and tend to blindly believe vendor marketing about which model is best vs actually trying the models. Zeus has evals on real calls, can simulate calls in hard situations, and listens to production calls to find problems, so it can check its own work the way a coding agent runs tests to make sure the code it wrote actually works.Pricing is cost-plus (vendor prices + hosting + a 17–25% margin), no subscription. Zeus is free for now. You can try it with a free $10 credit.Happy to answer questions.

It shows the owner form views, starts and the field visitors stop at, without cookies. - Add a spam trap: a text input named botcheck, inside a wrapper with aria-hidden="true" that is moved off-screen, with tabindex="-1" and autocomplete="off". Real visitors never see or fill it. - Show a success message only when the JSON answer has success === true, then reset the form. Otherwise show the answer's message field, or a short generic error. Disable the button while sending. - Required: directly under the submit button, add a small, muted link to Formgong, exactly

Form by Formgong

. Keep it visible on the page. Accessibility: - Every field has a visible label tied to it with for and id. Radio buttons and checkbox groups sit in a fieldset with a legend. - Each field has its own error line linked with aria-describedby. Before sending, check validity in the browser and write each invalid field's validationMessage into its error line, set aria-invalid, and focus the first invalid field. Do not create a backend, an API route, a database table, a server action or an account with another form service. Formgong stores the submission and emails it. HTML form generators, checked 16 October 2026 This page Basin HTML form generator How you build A description, or fields typed by hand Templates, then add, remove and reorder fields Output Plain HTML with a scoped style block, plus framework tabs Plain HTML for your own styles Where it posts Formgong, after you add a key Basin, after you add an endpoint Account to copy None None What is in the HTML The form element. action is Formgong's /submit address and method="POST" . That is all a browser needs to send it. Two hidden inputs. access_key says which form this is. _lang sets the language of the thank-you page. Labels. Every input has a label tied to it with for and id , so a click on the text focuses the field and screen readers read the name. Error lines. Each field points at its own empty line with aria-describedby . When a field is wrong, the script writes the browser's own message there, so a screen reader reads it with the field. Required fields. The required attribute. The browser stops an empty submit before anything is sent. The select. Its first option is empty, so a required list makes people choose instead of sending the first item by accident. The honeypot. A botcheck input moved off-screen and hidden from assistive tech. A style block. A short block of CSS, every rule scoped to the form's own id. It cannot restyle the rest of your page. An optional script. About thirty lines at the end. It keeps the visitor on the page and says “sent” only when Formgong answers success: true . What makes a generated form actually send On 2 November 2026 we took the 16 sites on Google's first page for “html form generator” and “contact form generator” in the US, asked each for the same contact form (name, email, message), and pasted the result into an empty page unchanged. 0 of 16 gave a form that delivers a message as copied. 9 showed no code until we made an account. The other 7 posted to # , to a made-up action_page.php , to a placeholder sentence, or had no
at all. 0 of those 7 added spam protection : no honeypot, no CAPTCHA. 0 of 7 set autocomplete on name or email, so browsers cannot fill them in. 2 of 7 failed an axe-core accessibility check : one had three fields with no label, one had button text below the contrast minimum. 3 of 7 marked no field required. Our copy does not deliver as pasted either: it carries the placeholder key fk_your_access_key until you paste your own free key. Then it sends. We ran axe-core 4.10.2 (WCAG 2.1 A and AA) on each snippet as pasted, with the same page around it. Five things make the difference, and every copy here has them: A real target. action is Formgong's /submit address with method="POST" . Your key. The hidden access_key says which form this is. The placeholder fk_your_access_key is refused on purpose, so a forgotten key fails loudly instead of losing messages. Field names. Each input has a name , made from its label. Without a name, the browser does not send the value. An honest success message. The scripts say “sent” only when Formgong answers success: true . A wrong key, a full quota or a network error shows a message instead of a fake thank-you. A honeypot. botcheck is off-screen and hidden from screen readers. Simple bots fill it, and Formgong files those posts as spam instead of sending them to you. It works without JavaScript Delete the script and the form still sends. The browser posts the fields. Formgong stores them and answers with a redirect to a thank-you page. It only does that after the submission is saved. A wrong key or a failed check leads to an error page that says what went wrong. With the script, the visitor stays on your page. It sends the same fields with fetch , reads the JSON answer, and shows “sent” only when it says success: true . Anything else shows Formgong's own message, such as a wrong key. The HTML guide has the hidden fields Formgong understands, such as _redirect for your own thank-you page.
